overview: This atlas record covers Sikkim from 1815 to 1878, during growing British intervention. Its single outline includes Darjeeling even after the 1835 cession, so it cannot represent changing borders accurately. The imported label “Indian princely state” is shorthand for changing relationships with British India, not membership in independent India. Sikkim’s kingdom and diverse communities had histories far beyond this map interval.

periods.title: War and territorial uncertainty
periods.summary: The Anglo-Nepal conflict preceded the Titalia settlement.

periods.title: The Titalia settlement
periods.summary: Territory was restored to Sikkim under a treaty with the East India Company.

periods.title: Darjeeling and further losses
periods.summary: The Darjeeling cession and later British annexation changed the kingdom’s southern frontier.

periods.title: After Tumlong
periods.summary: A new treaty imposed extensive British controls while the monarchy continued.

items.text: The 1817 Treaty of Titalia restored hill territory between the Mechi and Teesta rivers to Sikkim’s ruler. It also required him to submit disputes to British arbitration and assist British troops. Restored territory therefore came with political obligations.

The 1861 Treaty of Tumlong followed a British invasion. Its clauses required support for a trade road and rest houses, permitted surveys, and limited dealings with neighboring states. These were concrete restrictions on royal authority, not merely a friendly exchange of promises.

Trade rules affected travelers as well as rulers. Tumlong capped customs on goods passing toward Tibet, Bhutan or Nepal at five percent and required a pass after payment. That piece of paperwork was meant to prevent another charge farther along the route.

sections.title: Homes, food, families and useful bamboo

items.text: During his late-1840s travels, Hooker described Lepcha workers making temporary waterproof shelters with leaf or bamboo thatch, plus tables and sleeping platforms, using heavy knives. A skilled builder could turn nearby plants into a furnished camp: flat-pack furniture, forest edition.

Hooker recorded bamboo stems used as water vessels and leaves used for roofing around Darjeeling. Some young shoots were eaten. Choosing the right bamboo mattered: a plant useful for a sturdy container was not necessarily the best one to split into fine strips.

His account of Lepcha families describes marriage arrangements involving either payments or labor for the bride’s family, followed by a public feast. Household work, farming and family obligations were closely connected. This is one outsider’s nineteenth-century report, not a rule for every family.

A surviving nineteenth-century Lepcha basket base is woven from light-brown and red bamboo strips. It is about twenty centimeters across and weighs only fifty-five grams. Light materials could still require careful, patient work: every strip had to fit the pattern.

The basket’s catalogue lists Sikkim or Darjeeling as possible origins, with question marks. Its collection history is unknown. This makes it valuable evidence of a named craft tradition, but it cannot tell us which household made it or exactly where that family lived.

sections.title: Health and learning, with dates attached

items.text: Hooker reported strong fear of smallpox and demand for vaccination in the Darjeeling area. Doctors Pearson and Campbell provided it. This belongs to the British settlement after the cession; it does not establish that every remote Sikkimese village had access to vaccination.

Buddhist teaching centers long predated the atlas’s opening. Sikkim’s ecclesiastical history connects their foundation with the royal consecration of 1642 and subsequent patronage. Monasteries linked learning, religious authority and government; this did not mean that every child attended a monastery.

Later developments must stay later: historian Alex McKay places the growth of Western-style schools within Sikkim from the 1880s, followed by a supply of locally trained medical workers. Those institutions belong beyond the map’s 1878 endpoint, not in its earliest villages.

Hooker’s plant collecting depended on Lepcha assistants who knew the forests, gathered specimens and dried them. Botanical discovery was collaborative labor. Plants newly described for European science were often already familiar to the people who helped the visiting botanist find them.

The first part of The Rhododendrons of the Sikkim-Himalaya appeared in 1849, while Hooker was still away. Walter Hood Fitch turned field sketches into published botanical pictures. A flower could travel as a dried specimen and a carefully painted scientific image.

Collecting was entangled with power. Sikkim’s leaders worried that surveying visitors could help outsiders control their country. Hooker and Campbell crossed a prohibited frontier and were imprisoned in 1849; British threats secured their release, followed by territorial punishment for Sikkim.

sections.title: A word for home, and continuing knowledge

items.text: Here is a Lepcha word printed in Mainwaring’s 1876 grammar: ᰜᰧᰶ, li in simplified Roman transcription, meaning “house.” The original page shows the Lepcha letters beside the English gloss. This is an attested nineteenth-century printed example, reproduced here with modern Unicode characters.

The same grammar distinguishes words for an older brother and older sister, while younger siblings can be specified with additional gender terms. A grammar book preserves more than rules for sentences: it can reveal distinctions speakers make when talking about their families.

Long after this map interval, Gangtok’s Namgyal Institute of Tibetology opened in 1958. Its collections preserve texts, printing blocks, paintings and ritual objects. These surviving materials connect historical learning with research by living communities, rather than treating Sikkim’s traditions as things that ended in 1878.

The institute added a Tibetan medicine department in 2018. That dated example shows continuing study of Sowa-Rigpa alongside changing educational institutions. It should not be mistaken for a nineteenth-century medical college or evidence that a historical remedy was clinically effective.

ending.text: The 1878 endpoint is only a break in this atlas record. Sikkim’s monarchy continued beyond it; much later, in 1975, Sikkim became a state of India. Its communities, languages, religious institutions and knowledge continued through those political changes.
